cim: Ban it or embrace it? Anne Arundel parents divided on artificial intelligence in schools.
cim_eredeti: Ban it or embrace it? Anne Arundel parents divided on artificial intelligence in schools.
szoveg_eredeti:
Anne Arundel County’s public school system has a big decision to make soon: ban students’ use of artificial intelligence or embrace it?

Superintendent Mark Bedell has been asking parents to tackle that question, along with what to do about cellphone use in schools, at a series of community meetings, with the last two planned for this week. Bedell organized the meeting series because he pledged to listen to community members’ feedback before making any AI policy recommendations of his own.

“We will learn how to adjust to this AI era, even though it has everyone a little nervous,” the superintendent said Thursday during a meeting at Southern High in Harwood.

The draft AI policy under consideration by Anne Arundel’s school board is light on specifics. It requires AI tools to be vetted for educational value before adoption and emphasizes that the technology may not replace employees’ duties. It also directs the district to establish expectations, conditions and limitations for students’ use of AI. The board is set to update and finalize the policy next month.

The roughly three dozen parents who gathered Thursday night expressed a mix of excitement and fear about the new technology. Some argued AI can’t and shouldn’t be avoided, even though students may use it to cheat. Others said it stifles creativity and has no place in schools.

Attendee Tamara Bauer said she loves AI and uses it often in her personal life. She’s a mom of two and the principal at the Center of Applied Technology South, an Edgewater high school offering job training. She said the district’s priority should be teaching students to use AI safely and appropriately.

“We have to show students, this is how your learning, your thinking, your experience will be compromised if you rely on this technology to do the work for you,” said Bauer, who attended the meeting with her son Levi, a fifth grader. He was the youngest kid there.

When Levi needs help with his math homework, Bauer said she sometimes scans his worksheets and feeds them into an AI model. Rather than ask it to show her the answer, she asks it to explain, step by step, how to find the answer. Then she helps guide her son to do the work. A child working alone would be less deliberative, she said.

In an interview, Bedell said a few themes have emerged from the meetings he’s attended. Many parents have asked the district to teach students how to use AI safely. Others have asked for AI to be banned outright for children in elementary and middle schools, just as cellphone use at school is banned for those grades.

Bedell conceded that he doesn’t know how to give older students access to AI and prevent them from using it to cheat.

“We’ve always been able to figure out how to put guardrails in for new technology,” he said. “For this technology, we just haven’t figured it out yet.”

Other parents have begged Bedell to keep AI out of their children’s schools altogether. A procession of speakers who testified at a board meeting last month all had the same message: Ban it.

“Why are we rushing to embrace AI blindly?” asked Hillary Klemmt, a parent affiliated with the Schools Beyond Screens coalition, which advocates for evidence-based education technology policies. “Why are we using children as guinea pigs when there is so much at stake?”

The final two meetings are scheduled for Tuesday and Thursday from 6 to 8 p.m. Families are invited to gather on Tuesday at Annapolis High and on Thursday at Meade High.

Jessica Calefati is an education investigative reporter at The Baltimore Banner. She covers the Anne Arundel County schools and Maryland's child welfare system.
